title: World Models Lack a Persistent State
hook: Today's video world models render great frames but treat the world like a tracking shot: look away and back, and off-screen events freeze instead of running on — the moon keeps orbiting unwatched.
key_points: A real world model needs an internal state that evolves over time, decoupled from what the camera observes.
Existing benchmarks reward fidelity, motion, and camera control — never whether the world keeps evolving while unobserved.
WRBench treats camera motion as an intervention on observability across 9,600 videos from 23 models.
Across all four control paradigms, models resume a returning target in its abandoned state rather than advancing the event.
content_html: "World model" is one of the hottest phrases in AI, often pitched as a step toward AGI. But this paper argues that modeling the world means more than generating convincing frames on demand: it requires an internal state that keeps evolving over time, decoupled from observation, so objects endure and events run to completion whether or not a camera is watching — much as the moon holds its orbit when no one is looking.
extra_html:
What they tested

The authors note that existing benchmarks reward surface properties — fidelity, motion, camera controllability — but never ask whether a generated world keeps evolving once unobserved. So they built WRBench, a diagnostic that treats camera motion as an intervention on observability: does the camera execute the requested move, does the scene stay continuous while in view, and does a returning target remain consistent with the event that was set in motion? Across 9,600 videos from 23 models spanning four control paradigms, one failure was stubborn: systems maintain the observed world as a tracking shot, resuming a returning target in the state where it was abandoned rather than advancing the event while it was unseen.

Why it matters

Crucially, the failure recurred across control paradigms, model families, and scale — so robust world-state evolution doesn't fall out of cleaner imagery, tighter control, or more parameters. The authors argue that the stability of the physical state kernel and the consistency of "worldlines" under viewpoint changes should become first-class design objectives, shifting the goal from how the next frame looks to how the world will actually unfold.

related.title: DreamerV3: Mastering Domains through World Models
related.hook: Instead of learning only from real experience, DreamerV3 builds a world model and practices inside its own imagination — one fixed config, 150+ tasks.

related.title: World Models Meet Language Models
related.hook: A world model can imagine what happens next; an LLM can reason about it. The hard part is knowing when to trust the daydream — and when the simulation is just plausible nonsense.

flashcards.prompt: What capability do current video world models lack, according to this paper?
flashcards.back_html: A persistent state core: an internal world state that keeps evolving even when unobserved. They render the observed world like a tracking shot, freezing off-camera events instead of advancing them.

flashcards.prompt: How does WRBench probe whether a world model maintains state?

choices.text: It treats camera motion as an intervention on observability, then checks if a returning target advanced while unseen
It only measures image sharpness and frame rate
It asks humans to rate how realistic single frames look

flashcards.explanation_html: WRBench moves the camera away and back, testing whether the off-screen event continued. Across 23 models and four control paradigms, targets resumed in their abandoned state — a failure that didn't go away with scale.
